arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Stephen Kinnaird argued the Kentucky Supreme Court rule was too restrictive of the Sixth Amendment.
The United States Government disavowed the restrictive rule announced by the Kentucky Supreme Court.
Justice Scalia questioned whether the Court should open a Pandora's box by restricting advice to deportation.
Justice Scalia asked about advice regarding custody loss, noting it is a serious consequence.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Padilla v. Kentucky asks if the Sixth Amendment requires lawyers to warn clients about deportation risks before a guilty plea.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on October 13, 2009.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 3, lines 7-17

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to require lawyers to advise clients about deportation risks.
the opposing side wants the Court to limit legal duties to general criminal advice.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 20, lines 31-1

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues the Sixth Amendment mandates specific advice on immigration consequences.
the opposing side argues that requiring such advice expands legal duties beyond traditional criminal defense.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Kennedy asked if contract law principles regarding mistake risk apply to this situation.
Justice Alito asked why the duty would limit to guilty pleas rather than trial verdicts with lesser consequences.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the scope of legal advice required for criminal pleas. It determines whether lawyers must explain immigration risks to clients. The outcome shapes the standard of care for criminal defense attorneys nationwide.
